Prop Edge Engine · NFL 2026 · Week 2

Week 2 Picks

Paper picks, logged before kickoff and scored Monday. The model has not yet shown it can beat the book in Week 1, so every pick here is an argument, not a promise. This is analysis, not advice.

Built Sun Sep 20, 8:17 am PDT from DraftKings odds captured 2026-09-20 at 08:09 ET. Next update: Friday Sep 11 evening, after the 4 pm ET injury report (Week 1 practice reports start Wed Sep 9). How the picks are made.

How to read this page
Paper picks. In Week 1 the engine's numbers were further from the results than the book's at every market, and the legs it called favorable hit less often than the price implied. The cause was roles: the engine works from last season's usage and the book knew this season's from camp. The fixes on the list (moving a ruled-out back's carries, using the book's line as a role signal, a quarterback-run term) are not built yet, so this week every candidate was checked by hand against Week 1 snap counts and touches, and anything whose role changed was dropped or held to Lean. One leg clears every test this week; eight are Leans. Logged before kickoff, scored Monday against results and closing lines.

Three views. Picks is the sheet: the legs worth a bet, each with its price, the chance the price implies and the chance the model gives it. Games has one card per game in DraftKings order: kickoff, venue, roof, total, spread, the kickoff forecast, the verdict, the pick and its checks, the book's main lines and the players the model covers. All odds is every ladder the book listed, every rung, beside the model's chance.

Verdicts. Play means we would bet it: our number says it hits more often than the price suggests, the player did it often enough last year to back that up, and the defense he faces does not argue against it. A Play also has to keep at least 10 points of edge in the worst case, meaning if the opposing defense repeats last season in full (the Sensitivity line on each pick). Lean means we like it but something real gets in the way, so we are not betting it and it stays out of parlays; if you bet it anyway, bet small. Pass means the price is fair or too short, so there is no bet.

Parlays. Legs in different games multiply exactly, so the slip price is the product of the leg prices. For legs in the same game DraftKings reprices for correlation, and the displayed price will be lower than the product shown.

Weather. Each card shows the roof and the kickoff-hour forecast: weather.gov when its hourly forecast reaches the kickoff (about 6.5 days out), Open-Meteo before that, each labelled with the source. Rain enters the model as a chance shared by everyone in the game; wind of 15 mph or more shortens the passing game; indoor games carry no weather term.

Players tables. QB is the passer expected to start ("new" marks a change from last season, which the model discounts). Role is the share of the team's pass plays the receiver ran a route on last season, plus expected carries for backs; it is the volume input the model uses. Snap percent is for reference.

The picks

Book says is how often the price says it should hit. Model says is how often we think it hits. When ours is higher, that gap is the whole reason to bet. Odds are DraftKings prices at capture and move.

Every leg carries its reasons as bullets. Singles first, then the same-game pairs that only make sense together.

  • Cincinnati's third receiver played 61% of the snaps in Week 1 with 3 targets and 2 catches, the rung this bet needs; he caught 2 or more in 8 of 15 games last season (53%). The price says 48 and the model 60.
  • Houston is the one defense in the league that allowed a 2-catch receiver game in every one of its 17 games last season, so the opponent does not cut against it; if Houston repeats last year in full the model still says 58, ten points over the price.
  • It is a Play by the engine's rule and by the Week 1 usage check, but a modest one: the return at about even money is small, and a third receiver's targets are the first to vanish if Cincinnati runs the ball with a lead.

Longer parlays across bet types (lottery tickets)

Cross-game slips built from the best-value leg in each game across every market, one leg per game, so the price is exactly the product of the legs. A leg qualifies only if it clears the model's 3-point bar in the 35% to 75% book band, is not a mover, carries no new-quarterback or teammate-absence flag, was not rejected in this week's review, and the player's own record last season at that rung is at least what the price asks. Every added leg multiplies both the payout and the chance of losing; these hit a few times a season at best.

How the picks are made

Each game is simulated thousands of times as one offense: the play count, the split between dropbacks and runs, every receiver's targets, catches and yards, every back's carries and yards, and the quarterback's passing line as the sum of what his receivers do plus the throws to everyone else. A quarterback's passing yards and his receiver's yards are therefore priced together, and a back's carries fall in the same simulated games where the passing volume rises.

Behind that sit every receiver's route share, target rate, depth of target, catch rate and yards per catch, both teams' tempo, the total and spread, venue, kickoff window and forecast. The opposing defense enters as five measured terms (yards per target, catch rate, passing touchdowns per attempt, yards per carry and rushing touchdowns per carry allowed, each relative to the league and shrunk hard because defense barely repeats year to year) plus the total and spread. Teammates share the game's pass volume, so paired legs are priced together. A leg makes the list only when the model's number beats the price by a clear margin, the player's own record supports it, and a plain-language reason survives. Games a teammate missed count at 30%, games under a different quarterback at 50%, deep rungs are excluded, and players on a new team are shown but never picked.

Verdict
LeanCade Otton (TB) 4+ receptions at +150. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
Cade Otton (TB) 4+ receptions at +150.
  • Tampa Bay's only every-down tight end: in Week 1 he played 98% of the snaps and drew 5 targets, catching 3, the same role he held all last season.
  • He caught 4 or more in 8 of 15 games last season (53%); the price says it happens fewer than four times in ten, and the model lands at 49.
  • The risk is game script, not role: Tampa Bay is an 8.5-point home favorite in a 41.5-total game, and a big lead means fewer throws. Baker Mayfield still threw 28 times in Week 1 with a lead for most of the day.
  • Held to Lean on Sunday morning's prices: Cleveland allowed a 4-catch tight end game in only 6 of 17 last season (third fewest), and if that defense repeats the model's 50 becomes 48 against a price of 40, two points short of the ten the Play rule asks for.
  • Opponent, with numbers: A tight end reached 4 catches against CLE in 6 of 17 games last year (league average 8.6; 3rd fewest of 32). CLE allowed 6.92 yards per target (7.38 league, 9th fewest of 32) and a 66.3% catch rate (67.5% league). CLE blitzed on 31% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Against defenses like CLE: the 8 closest to CLE's pass defense last season, judged on yards per attempt, completion rate, sack rate, touchdowns per attempt, blitz rate. yards per attempt allowed: CLE 6.57, league 7.04; the group: NO 6.81, LA 6.75, DET 7.23, ATL 7.17, BUF 6.31, LAC 6.61, NE 6.66, HOU 6.47. He reached 4 catches against that group in 2025: 4 of 8 (0, 3, 7, 4, 9, 2, 4, 3); 2024: 1 of 5 (0, 3, 2, 9, 2). Every tight end against that group last season reached 4 catches in 22 games of 100, against 28 versus everyone else and 17 against CLE itself.
  • By tier: CLE's pass defense was top ten last season on yards per attempt allowed. His record by defense tier, top ten: 2 of 5 in 2025 (3, 3, 4, 9, 2); 4 of 6 in 2024 (7, 6, 3, 9, 5, 2); middle twelve: 4 of 7 in 2025 (0, 5, 7, 4, 4, 2, 3); 2 of 5 in 2024 (1, 0, 8, 8, 3); bottom ten: 2 of 3 in 2025 (2, 4, 7); 1 of 3 in 2024 (2, 1, 4). Every tight end last season reached 4 catches against top-ten defenses 24 times in 100, middle twelve 26, bottom ten 28.
  • Worst case: Model 50 in 100 as built. If CLE's defense repeats last season in full, 49. The price says 40. Holds in the worst case.

LeanTreVeyon Henderson (NE) 40+ rushing yards at +126. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
TreVeyon Henderson (NE) 40+ rushing yards at +126.
  • He cleared 40 in 9 of 17 games last season as New England's lead back, and the model has 58 against a price of 44, 58 in the worst case too. The price has drifted from +114 on Friday to +126 this morning: the market is pricing a smaller share for him, which is the same doubt that holds this to Lean.
  • Held to Lean: he missed Week 1, and in his absence Rhamondre Stevenson played 85% of the snaps with 18 carries and 5 catches. How the carries split in his first game back is exactly the kind of role question the engine got wrong last week.
  • Opponent, with numbers: PIT allowed 4.27 yards per carry last year against a league average of 4.38 (14th fewest of 32), 113 rushing yards a game against 116, and the opposing lead back reached 40 yards in 13 of 17 games (league average 13.5; 9th fewest of 32). Neutral for this leg.
  • Against defenses like PIT: the 8 closest to PIT's run defense last season, judged on yards per carry, rushing yards per game, rushing touchdowns per carry, how often the lead back reached 60. yards per carry allowed: PIT 4.27, league 4.37; the group: CLE 4.07, MIN 3.99, GB 4.23, LA 4.38, SF 4.34, ATL 4.68, KC 4.03, NO 3.97. He reached 40 rushing yards against that group in 2025: 2 of 3 (27, 75, 55). Every back against that group last season reached 40 rushing yards in 42 games of 100, against 38 versus everyone else and 33 against PIT itself.
  • By tier: PIT's run defense was middle twelve last season on yards per carry allowed. His record by defense tier, top ten: 1 of 3 in 2025 (27, 27, 75); middle twelve: 1 of 5 in 2025 (28, 32, 5, 147, 3); bottom ten: 7 of 9 in 2025 (10, 24, 55, 62, 66, 67, 148, 82, 53). Every back last season reached 40 rushing yards against top-ten defenses 37 times in 100, middle twelve 37, bottom ten 42.
  • Worst case: Model 58 in 100 as built. If PIT's defense repeats last season in full, 56. The price says 44. Holds in the worst case.

Verdict
LeanJacoby Brissett (ARI) 240+ passing yards at +153; Michael Wilson (ARI) 50+ receiving yards at +176. The model is ahead of the price but the football case has a hole; see the reasons below.
The lean
Jacoby Brissett (ARI) 240+ passing yards at +153.
  • Kyler Murray is out with a concussion, so Brissett starts a second straight game. In Week 1 he threw 37 times for 277 yards, and as a starter last season he cleared 240 in 10 of 14 games (71%); the price says 39.
  • Held to Lean: Seattle's defense is the reason. If it plays to last season's numbers, the model's 52 drops to 32, under the price of 40. Seattle held Drake Maye to 178 last week.
  • Opponent, with numbers: SEA allowed 212.88 passing yards a game last year against a league average of 224.68 (12th fewest of 32), 6.03 yards per attempt (7.02 league, 1st fewest of 32) while facing 35.3 attempts a game (32.0 league), and a quarterback reached 240 against them in 6 of 17 games (league average 6.9; 13th fewest of 32). SEA blitzed on 28% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. A real minus for this leg.
  • Against defenses like SEA: the 8 closest to SEA's pass defense last season, judged on yards per attempt, completion rate, sack rate, touchdowns per attempt, blitz rate. yards per attempt allowed: SEA 6.06, league 7.04; the group: LAC 6.61, BUF 6.31, HOU 6.47, LA 6.75, GB 6.41, JAX 6.16, PHI 6.44, NE 6.66. The lean
Matthew Stafford (LA) 270+ passing yards at +173.
  • He threw for 270 or more in 9 of 17 games last season; the price says fewer than four in ten and the model says 63. Monday night at home against a Giants defense that let Dallas move the ball on the ground rather than through the air.
  • Held to Lean, not Play: Week 1 was 155 yards on 25 attempts in a 27 to 7 loss, and Puka Nacua is questionable with a hip injury after missing Friday's practice. If Nacua sits, this comes off the sheet.
  • Opponent, with numbers: NYG allowed 228.76 passing yards a game last year against a league average of 224.68 (16th most of 32), 7.08 yards per attempt (7.02 league, 15th most of 32) while facing 32.3 attempts a game (32.0 league), and a quarterback reached 270 against them in 5 of 17 games (league average 4.4; 12th most of 32). NYG blitzed on 35% of dropbacks (league 30%); blitzing raises sacks and touchdown passes and lowers completions, and the model applies that mix. Neutral for this leg.
  • Against defenses like NYG: the 8 closest to NYG's pass defense last season, judged on yards per attempt, completion rate, sack rate, touchdowns per attempt, blitz rate. yards per attempt allowed: NYG 7.12, league 7.04; the group: IND 7.21, PIT 7.24, CAR 7.31, NE 6.66, KC 6.92, ARI 7.24, NO 6.81, LA 6.75.   • By tier: NYG's pass defense was middle twelve last season on yards per attempt allowed. His record by defense tier, top ten: 1 of 5 in 2025 (245, 196, 182, 130, 457); 2 of 6 in 2024 (221, 298, 293, 243, 160, 110); middle twelve: 6 of 9 in 2025 (375, 389, 181, 281, 280, 281, 368, 269, 259); 4 of 6 in 2024 (317, 260, 154, 279, 295, 320); bottom ten: 2 of 3 in 2025 (298, 273, 243); 0 of 4 in 2024 (216, 224, 183, 189).
